title: Objective Morality
rootClaim: Objective moral facts exist independently of human opinions, cultural beliefs, individual attitudes, or evolutionary conditioning.

branches.text: Moral Intuition & Universal Convergence: First-person moral experience and cross-cultural consensus provide direct prima facie evidence of stance-independent moral facts.

children.text: Moral Intuitionism: Fundamental moral truths are self-evident rational intuitions apprehended directly, functioning analogously to mathematical or logical axioms.

Evolutionary Debunking Argument: Natural selection shaped human moral intuitions strictly for survival and reproductive fitness, rendering their alignment with stance-independent moral facts an ungrounded coincidence.

Normative Tracking & Evolutionary Reliability: Abstract reasoning in mathematics and logic evolved under identical adaptive pressures yet tracks objective truth; moral cognition similarly utilizes generalized rational faculties.
Cultural Relativism & Diversity: Moral codes vary radically across history and civilizations, indicating that moral standards are socio-cultural constructs rather than objective discoveries.

Surface Diversity vs. Core Consensus: Surface moral variations stem from differing empirical beliefs or environmental constraints, whereas core principles (prohibiting arbitrary murder, protecting children, reciprocal fairness) exhibit universal agreement.
Moral Progress Argument: Historical developments—such as the global abolition of slavery and expansion of universal human rights—represent genuine objective progress toward a moral truth benchmark.

Social Power Realignment: Perceived 'moral progress' merely reflects changing economic structures, technological capabilities, and shifts in dominant socio-political power rather than convergence on an external moral benchmark.

branches.text: Rational Deontology & Universal Imperatives: Moral duties are derived directly from the requirements of practical reason, which obligates all rational agents universally.

children.text: Universalizability Principle: An action is morally permissible if and only if its underlying maxim can be consistently willed as a universal law without generating a logical or practical contradiction.

Is-Ought Problem: Descriptive premises about what 'is' (natural facts or logical principles) cannot yield prescriptive premises about what 'ought' to be done without smuggling in unproven normative claims.

Constitutivism & Agency: Rational agency possesses constitutive aims; engaging in deliberation logically commits agents to valuing their own agency and, by rational consistency, the agency of all rational beings.

branches.text: Transcendental & Ontological Grounding: Objective moral obligations require an immutable, transcendent foundation—such as a necessary supreme nature—to establish objective value and authoritative duty.

children.text: Divine Command & Moral Duty: Absent a transcendent personal source to ground binding moral commands, moral values reduce to subjective aesthetic preferences or biological imperatives.
Euthyphro Dilemma: If actions are good solely because God commands them, morality is arbitrary; if God commands them because they are inherently good, morality is independent of divine authority.
Modified Divine Command Theory: God's immutable, perfectly good nature—rather than arbitrary divine choice or an external law—serves as the foundational standard of moral goodness.

branches.text: Moral Anti-Realism & Emotivism: Moral statements do not express objective propositions about reality; they express subjective emotional reactions, social attitudes, or prescriptive desires.

children.text: Emotivism & Expressivism: Declarations like 'Cruelty is wrong' are not true-or-false factual assertions, but emotional expressions equivalent to saying 'Boo to cruelty!' or issuing personal imperatives.

Frege-Geach Embedding Problem: Moral statements function syntactically and logically in unasserted conditional premises (e.g., 'If lying is wrong, then getting others to lie is wrong'), which non-cognitivist expressivism fails to explain without logical equivocation.
Subjective Constructivism: Moral values are valid only relative to individual preferences or social contracts, possessing no stance-independent status in the natural world.
Disagreement Paradox: If moral subjectivism were accurate, individuals with opposing moral views would not actually be disagreeing, but merely stating separate psychological facts about themselves.

branches.text: Moral Error Theory & Metaphysical Queerness: Moral claims attempt to assert objective facts, but because objective prescriptivity is incompatible with naturalism, all positive moral assertions are false.

children.text: Argument from Queerness: Objective moral values would have to be entities of a bizarre non-natural type—combining objective properties with intrinsic motivational direction—requiring an unexplainable faculty of moral intuition.

Companions in Guilt Argument: Epistemic norms (such as logical consistency, empirical evidence, and cognitive justification) are equally unobservable and prescriptive; denying objective moral facts logically forces the rejection of objective rational standards.
Explanatory Superfluity: Science and evolutionary biology fully account for the existence of human moral beliefs and behaviors without postulating real moral facts.

definitions.description: The metaethical view that objective moral facts exist independently of human beliefs, desires, feelings, or social conventions.
The position that there are no objective moral facts; moral values are subjective, socially constructed, or non-existent.
A metaethical stance asserting that moral statements purport to express objective truths, but because objective moral values do not exist, all positive moral claims are strictly false.
J.L. Mackie's argument that objective moral values would be metaphysically entity-types unlike anything else in the universe and would require an epistemologically peculiar faculty of intuition.
An argument claiming that because evolutionary forces selected human moral intuitions for survival rather than truth-tracking, our moral beliefs lack epistemic justification.
Socrates' famous challenge asking whether an action is morally good because a deity commands it, or whether a deity commands it because the action is inherently morally good.
David Hume's observation that logical deductions cannot move from purely descriptive claims about what 'is' to prescriptive claims about what 'ought' to be without additional normative premises.
A challenge for moral expressivism explaining how moral terms retain valid logic and meaning when embedded in unasserted conditional statements.
Immanuel Kant's foundational deontological principle requiring that one act only according to maxims that can be consistently willed as universal laws.
A defense of moral realism showing that attacks on moral facts (such as non-naturalism or prescriptivity) equally apply to epistemic norms, which all rational discourse requires.
A non-cognitivist theory holding that moral statements do not state facts, but rather express emotional attitudes or feelings of approval or disapproval.
The epistemological view that foundational moral truths can be apprehended directly through rational moral intuition without needing empirical proof.
